resposta:
**Secretários de Saúde e Serviços Humanos dos Estados Unidos (de 1 janeiro 2018 até 31 dezembro 2024)**  

| # | Nome completo | Tipo (regular / interino) | Início da função | Fim da função* | Partido (se aplicável) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Alex M. Azar II** (Alex Azar) | Secretário (cabine) | 29 de janeiro 2018 | 20 de janeiro 2021 | Democrata |
| 2 | **Norris Cochran** | Interino (secretário executivo) | 20 de janeiro 2021 | 19 de março 2021 | Independente |
| 3 | **Xavier Becerra** | Secretário (cabine) | 19 de março 2021 | 20 de janeiro 2025 (entrou em vigor em 18 março 2021) | Democrata |

\*Para Xavier Becerra, o mandato termina em 20 de janeiro 2025; portanto, durante todo o período de 2022 a 2024 ele foi o único secretário da Casa Branca nessa data.

### Observações
- **Alex Azar** assumiu em 29 de janeiro 2018 e permaneceu até ser substituído por Norris Cochran.
- **Norris Cochran** serviu como *acting* secretário apenas entre 20 de janeiro 2021 e 19 de março 2021, quando Xavier Becerra tomou posse.
- **Xavier Becerra** foi confirmado pelo Senado em 18 de março 2021 e juramentado em 22 de março 2021; seu mandato continua até 20 de janeiro 2025, cobrindo integralmente o ano de 2024.
- Após o término de Becerra (20 de janeiro 2025), Dorothy Fink foi nomeada *acting* secretário (de 20 de janeiro 2025 a 13 de fevereiro 2025), mas esse período está fora do intervalo solicitado (2024).

### Fontes
- **Wikipedia – United States Secretary of Health and Human Services**: lista de secretários com datas de ingresso/saída.  
  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services  
- **Chronologia de secretários (NIH)**: mostra os períodos de cada secretário.  
  https://www.nih.gov/about-nih/nih-almanac/department-health-human-services-secretaries  
- **Norris Cochran – Wikipedia**: “Acting United States Secretary of Health and Human Services” (20 jan 2021 – 19 mar 2021).  
  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran  
- **Xavier Becerra – Wikipedia**: “In office March 19 2021 – January 20 2025”.  
  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra  
- **Dorothy Fink – Wikipedia**: “Acting United States Secretary of Health and Human Services” (20 jan 2025 – 13 feb 2025).  
  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink  

Essas três pessoas são os únicos ocupantes da posição entre 1 janeiro 2018 e 31 dezembro 2024, incluindo o interino Norris Cochran.

The **United States secretary of health and human services** is the head of the [United States Department of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Department of Health and Human Services"), and serves as the principal advisor to the [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") on health matters. The secretary is a member of the [United States Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Cabinet "United States Cabinet"). [Robert F. Kennedy Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_F._Kennedy_Jr. "Robert F. Kennedy Jr.") is the incumbent secretary of health and human services, having held the position since February 13, 2025.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-2)

The office was formerly known as the secretary of health, education, and welfare. In 1980, the [Department of Health, Education, and Welfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health,_Education,_and_Welfare "United States Department of Health, Education, and Welfare") was renamed to Department of Health and Human Services, and its education functions and [Rehabilitation Services Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rehabilitation_Services_Administration "Rehabilitation Services Administration") were transferred to the new [United States Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-3) [Patricia Roberts Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patricia_Roberts_Harris "Patricia Roberts Harris") headed the department before and after it was renamed.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-4)

Nominations to the office are referred to the [Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Health,_Education,_Labor,_and_Pensions "United States Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions") and the [United States Senate Committee on Finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Finance "United States Senate Committee on Finance"), which has jurisdiction over Medicare and Medicaid,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-5) before confirmation is considered by the full [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"). The secretary of health and human services is a [level I position in the Executive Schedule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Schedule#Level_I "Executive Schedule"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-6) thus earning a salary of [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Dollar "US Dollar")250,600, as of January 2025.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-Salary-7)

## Duties

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Flag_of_the_Secretary_of_Health%2C_Education%2C_and_Welfare.png/250px-Flag_of_the_Secretary_of_Health%2C_Education%2C_and_Welfare.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flag_of_the_Secretary_of_Health,_Education,_and_Welfare.png)The flag of the secretary of health, education, and welfare, the predecessor to the current office

The duties of the secretary revolve around human conditions and concerns in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"). This includes advising the [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") on matters of [health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health "Health"), [welfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_security "Social security"), and income security programs. The secretary strives to administer the Department of Health and Human Services to carry out approved programs and make the public aware of the objectives of the department.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-8)

The [Department of Health, Education and Welfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health,_Education,_and_Welfare "United States Department of Health, Education, and Welfare") (HEW) was reorganized into a [Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education") and a [Department of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Department of Health and Human Services") (HHS).

The Department of Health and Human Services oversees 11 agencies including the [Food and Drug Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_Drug_Administration "Food and Drug Administration") (FDA), [Centers for Disease Control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control "Centers for Disease Control") (CDC), [National Institutes of Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institutes_of_Health "National Institutes of Health") (NIH), [Administration for Children and Families](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administration_for_Children_and_Families "Administration for Children and Families") (ACF) and [Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Medicare_and_Medicaid_Services "Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services") (CMS).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-9)

The line of succession for the secretary of health and human services is as follows:[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-11)

1. [Deputy Secretary of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Deputy_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Deputy Secretary of Health and Human Services").
2. General Counsel of the Department of Health and Human Services
3. Assistant Secretary for Administration
4. [Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assistant_Secretary_for_Planning_and_Evaluation "Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation")
5. Administrator of the [Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Medicare_and_Medicaid_Services "Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services")
6. [Commissioner of Food and Drugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commissioner_of_Food_and_Drugs "Commissioner of Food and Drugs")
7. Director of the [National Institutes of Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institutes_of_Health "National Institutes of Health")
8. Assistant Secretary for [Children and Families](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administration_for_Children_and_Families "Administration for Children and Families")
9. Other assistant secretaries (following in the order they took the oath of office)
  1. [Assistant Secretary for Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Assistant_Secretary_for_Health "United States Assistant Secretary for Health")
  2. [Assistant Secretary for Preparedness and Response](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_the_Assistant_Secretary_for_Preparedness_and_Response "Office of the Assistant Secretary for Preparedness and Response")
  3. Assistant Secretary for Legislation
  4. Assistant Secretary for Public Affairs
  5. Assistant Secretary for Financial Resources
  6. Assistant Secretary for [Aging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administration_on_Aging "Administration on Aging")
10. Director of the [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control_and_Prevention "Centers for Disease Control and Prevention")
11. Director, Region 4 ([Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta "Atlanta"), [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)"))

**Norris Whitehouse Cochran IV** (born June 9, 1970) is an American government official who served as the acting [United States Secretary of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Secretary of Health and Human Services") from January to March 2021, having also served in this role previously in 2017.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran#cite_note-1) He serves as Deputy Assistant Secretary of Budget, and was Acting Assistant Secretary for Financial Resources in the [United States Department of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Department of Health and Human Services") throughout most of the Trump administration.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran#cite_note-2)

## Education and career

Cochran received a [B.A.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") from the [University of California, Santa Barbara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Santa_Barbara "University of California, Santa Barbara") in history of public policy in 1993.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran#cite_note-:0-5) He earned a [Master of Public Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Public_Affairs "Master of Public Affairs") at the [University of Texas at Austin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Austin "University of Texas at Austin")'s [Lyndon B. Johnson School of Public Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson_School_of_Public_Affairs "Lyndon B. Johnson School of Public Affairs") in 1995.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran#cite_note-:0-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran#cite_note-6)

Cochran first worked for the federal government in 1996 when he joined the [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control_and_Prevention "Centers for Disease Control and Prevention"). Between 2001 and 2006 he worked for the Health Division of the [Office of Management and Budget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_Management_and_Budget "Office of Management and Budget").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran#cite_note-:0-5)

On February 5, 2006, he joined the [Department of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Department of Health and Human Services").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran#cite_note-:0-5) As of 2007, he was the Director of the Division of Discretionary Programs.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran#cite_note-7) He has been Deputy Assistant Secretary of Budget, a [Senior Executive Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senior_Executive_Service_(United_States) "Senior Executive Service (United States)") position, since March 2009.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran#cite_note-9) This position involves being the Director of the HHS Office of Budget.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norris_Cochran#cite_note-:0-5)

**Xavier Becerra** ([/ˌhɑːviˈɛər bəˈsɛrə/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); Spanish: [[xaˈβjeɾ beˈsera]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish"); born January 26, 1958) is an American attorney and politician who served as the 25th [United States secretary of health and human services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_secretary_of_health_and_human_services "United States secretary of health and human services") under President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") from 2021 to 2025. A member of the [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)"), Becerra previously served as the 33rd [attorney general of California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attorney_general_of_California "Attorney general of California") from 2017 to 2021 and as a [U.S. representative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") from [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California") from 1993 to 2017. He has advanced to the [2026 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_gubernatorial_election "2026 California gubernatorial election") for [governor of California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_California "Governor of California"), where he will face [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") candidate [Steve Hilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Hilton "Steve Hilton").

Becerra was born and raised in [Sacramento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento,_California "Sacramento, California") and received [Bachelor of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") and [Juris Doctor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juris_Doctor "Juris Doctor") degrees from [Stanford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University"). He worked as an administrative assistant for state senator [Art Torres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Torres "Art Torres") and as a deputy attorney general in the [California Department of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Department_of_Justice "California Department of Justice") in the late 1980s. He served in the [California State Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_Assembly "California State Assembly") from 1990 to 1992.

First elected to the U.S. House of Representatives in [1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_California "1992 United States House of Representatives elections in California"), Becerra chaired the [Congressional Hispanic Caucus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Hispanic_Caucus "Congressional Hispanic Caucus") from 1997 to 1999 and the [House Democratic Caucus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_Democratic_Caucus "House Democratic Caucus") from 2013 to 2017. In 2017, Governor [Jerry Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Brown "Jerry Brown") appointed Becerra to replace [Kamala Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris") as attorney general after Harris was [elected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_Senate_election_in_California "2016 United States Senate election in California") to the [U.S. Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"). He was elected to a full term in [2018](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_California_Attorney_General_election "2018 California Attorney General election") and served until he joined the [Biden cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_Joe_Biden "Cabinet of Joe Biden") in 2021.

## Early life and education

Becerra was born on January 26, 1958, in [Sacramento, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento,_California "Sacramento, California").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-1) He is the son of Maria Teresa and Manuel Guerrero Becerra. His father was born in Sacramento and raised in [Tijuana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tijuana "Tijuana"), [Baja California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baja_California "Baja California"), Mexico, and later moved back to the U.S. as a teenager. His mother was from [Guadalajara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guadalajara "Guadalajara"), [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-2) Becerra grew up in a one-room apartment with his three sisters.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-3) He graduated in 1976 from [C. K. McClatchy High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._K._McClatchy_High_School "C. K. McClatchy High School").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-4) He studied abroad at the [University of Salamanca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Salamanca "University of Salamanca") in Spain from 1978 to 1979 and earned his Bachelor of Arts in economics from [Stanford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University") in 1980, becoming the [first person in his family to graduate from college](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-generation_college_students_in_the_United_States "First-generation college students in the United States").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-7) He received his [Juris Doctor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juris_Doctor "Juris Doctor") from [Stanford Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Law_School "Stanford Law School") in 1984 and was admitted to the [State Bar of California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Bar_of_California "State Bar of California") in 1985.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-8)

## Early career

As an attorney, Becerra worked on cases involving individuals who had mental disorders for the Legal Assistance Corporation of Central Massachusetts[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-9) (now Community Legal Aid).

Becerra returned to California, and in 1986, became an administrative assistant for Democratic [State Senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_Senate "California State Senate") [Art Torres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Torres "Art Torres") of Los Angeles.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-10) He served as a deputy attorney general in the [California Department of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Department_of_Justice "California Department of Justice") under [Attorney General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Attorney_General "California Attorney General") [John Van de Kamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Van_de_Kamp "John Van de Kamp") from 1987 to 1990.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-11)

After incumbent state assemblymember [Charles Calderon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Calderon "Charles Calderon") decided to seek a seat in the California Senate, Becerra launched a campaign for the [California State Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_Assembly "California State Assembly"), defeating Calderon's Senate aide Marta Maestas in the Democratic primary.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-12) He went on to defeat [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") Lee Lieberg and [Libertarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libertarian_Party_(United_States) "Libertarian Party (United States)") Steven Pencall, receiving 60% of the vote.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-13) Becerra served one term in the State Assembly, representing California's 59th district, from 1990 to 1992.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-14)

## U.S. House of Representatives (1993–2017)

### Elections

In 1992, Becerra won the Democratic primary in [California's 30th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California's_30th_congressional_district "California's 30th congressional district") with a plurality of 32% of the vote.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-15) In the general election, he defeated Republican nominee Morry Waksberg, 58%–24%.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-16) He won re-election to a second term in 1994 with 66%[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-17) of the vote. His district was renumbered as the [31st district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California's_31st_congressional_district "California's 31st congressional district") after the 2000 census.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

After redistricting, ahead of the [2012 elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_California,_2012 "United States House of Representatives elections in California, 2012"), most of Becerra's old district became the [34th district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California's_34th_congressional_district "California's 34th congressional district"). He defeated Republican Stephen Smith 85.6% to 14.4%.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-18)

### Tenure

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Xavier_Beccarra%2C_2004.jpg/250px-Xavier_Beccarra%2C_2004.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Xavier_Beccarra,_2004.jpg)Official portrait, 2004[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/President_Bill_Clinton%2C_Tipper_Gore%2C_and_Xavier_Becerra.jpg/250px-President_Bill_Clinton%2C_Tipper_Gore%2C_and_Xavier_Becerra.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:President_Bill_Clinton,_Tipper_Gore,_and_Xavier_Becerra.jpg)[Tipper Gore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tipper_Gore "Tipper Gore") (left), Becerra (center), and President [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton")

Becerra was a member of the [Congressional Hispanic Caucus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Hispanic_Caucus "Congressional Hispanic Caucus"), of which he served as chair during the [105th Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/105th_Congress "105th Congress").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-19)

Becerra was appointed assistant to the speaker of the House for the 110th Congress.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-20) He won his bid to succeed [John Larson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Larson "John Larson") as [vice chair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Caucus_Vice-Chairman_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives "Democratic Caucus Vice-Chairman of the United States House of Representatives") in the 111th Congress, defeating [Marcy Kaptur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcy_Kaptur "Marcy Kaptur") of Ohio by a vote of 175–67.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-21) Becerra successfully ran for a second term as vice chair in 2011 to serve during the [112th Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/112th_Congress "112th Congress").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-22) He served as chair of the House Democratic Caucus from 2013 to 2017.

#### Abortion rights

Becerra voted against H.R. 3541, the Prenatal Non-Discrimination Act (PRENDA), which would have imposed civil and criminal penalties on anyone knowingly attempting to perform a [sex-selective abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex-selective_abortion "Sex-selective abortion").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-23)

Becerra argued before the [United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Ninth_Circuit "United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit") that the [Little Sisters of the Poor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Sisters_of_the_Poor "Little Sisters of the Poor"), a Catholic religious order, should be required to provide [birth control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_control "Birth control") services under the [Affordable Care Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affordable_Care_Act "Affordable Care Act").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-24) In late 2020, arguing that the prosecution would discourage pregnant women from obtaining addiction treatment, Becerra urged the California Supreme Court to drop a murder charge against Chelsea Becker, a woman who had been arrested following a stillbirth in which methamphetamine was found in the fetus's system. He contended that the state's murder statute was intended to protect pregnant women from third-party violence, not to criminalize them for the outcomes of their own pregnancies.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-25)

#### 2001 Los Angeles mayoral election

Main article: [2001 Los Angeles mayoral election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Los_Angeles_mayoral_election "2001 Los Angeles mayoral election")

Becerra ran for mayor of Los Angeles in 2001. He finished with 6% of the primary vote.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Herszenhorn-26)

#### Consideration for federal government positions

In 2008, Becerra was considered for the position of [U.S. trade representative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._trade_representative "U.S. trade representative") in the administration of President-elect Obama.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-27) While it was reported that he had already accepted,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-28) he announced on December 15 that he would not accept the position.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-29)

Becerra was on the shortlist of presumptive Democratic presidential nominee [Hillary Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Clinton "Hillary Clinton") for the [vice presidential nomination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Democratic_Party_vice_presidential_candidate_selection "2016 Democratic Party vice presidential candidate selection") in 2016.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Herszenhorn-26)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-30) Senator [Tim Kaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Kaine "Tim Kaine") was eventually chosen.

## California attorney general (2017–2021)

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Xavier_Becerra_official_portrait.jpg/250px-Xavier_Becerra_official_portrait.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Xavier_Becerra_official_portrait.jpg)Official portrait, 2017

On January 24, 2017, upon appointment by California governor [Jerry Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Brown "Jerry Brown"), Becerra took office and became the first Latino to serve as California's attorney general.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-33) Becerra was elected to a full four-year term in [2018](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_California_Attorney_General_election "2018 California Attorney General election"), defeating Republican Steven Bailey with 63% of the vote.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-34) He delivered the Democratic Spanish-language response to President Trump's 2019 [State of the Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_the_Union "State of the Union") address.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-35)

During his term as attorney general, Becerra filed 122 lawsuits against the first Trump administration.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-37)

### California Department of Justice reforms

#### Bureau of Environmental Justice

In 2018, Becerra created an [environmental justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_justice "Environmental justice") bureau at the California Department of Justice. It opposed the effort to expand [San Bernardino International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Bernardino_International_Airport "San Bernardino International Airport") due to concerns regarding [air pollution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_pollution_in_the_United_States "Air pollution in the United States"), intervened to halt a proposed waterfront cement plant in Vallejo, citing significant concerns over increased air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions, and supported the City of Arvin's oil and gas ordinance, endorsing a 300-foot buffer for homes, schools, and hospitals.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-39)

#### Protection of endangered species in Sacramento and San Joaquin River

On May 11, 2020, Becerra secured a preliminary injunction in this lawsuit against the Trump Administration for unlawfully expanding water export operations in the Central Valley.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-40)

### Criminal law enforcement

On June 4, 2019, Becerra announced the arrest of [Naasón Joaquín García](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naasón_Joaquín_García "Naasón Joaquín García"), leader of the Mexican [megachurch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megachurch "Megachurch") [La Luz Del Mundo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Luz_Del_Mundo "La Luz Del Mundo") and other co-defendants. Charges included human trafficking, production of child pornography, and forcible rape of a minor. On June 8, 2022, Naasón Joaquín García was sentenced to more than 16 years in a California prison.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-41) In the same year, Becerra filed charges against a number of men for their alleged involvement in a statewide organized crime ring engaged in sex trafficking, tax fraud, and money laundering. Five suspects were sentenced in March 2022.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-42)

Becerra brought fourteen felony charges against [Center for Medical Progress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_for_Medical_Progress "Center for Medical Progress") activists for [secretly recording fourteen videos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_Parenthood_2015_undercover_videos_controversy "Planned Parenthood 2015 undercover videos controversy"), and one felony charge for conspiring to invade privacy, on March 28, 2017.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-43) Two members of the group pleaded no contest to a felony each in 2025.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-44) In August 2018, an operation targeted the [MS-13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MS-13 "MS-13") gang in the [Central Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Valley_(California) "Central Valley (California)") and beyond. The following year, multiple operations were directed against Norteño street gangs in Kings, Tulare, and Stanislaus Counties, as well as in Stockton.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-45) In December 2019, the Country Boy Crips in south [Bakersfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bakersfield "Bakersfield") were the focus of a significant operation.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-46)

In December 2020, Becerra was faulted by state district attorneys for not taking leadership to help stop unemployment fraud during the COVID-19 pandemic, in what was described as the "biggest taxpayer fraud in California history".[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Chabria-47) In January 2021, investigators said the total fraud was over $11 billion, with $19 billion in claims still under investigation.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-50) Most of this money will likely never be recovered, prosecutors said.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Chabria-47)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-52)

### Transparency

In 2019, Becerra threatened legal action against reporters who had received records of California law enforcement officers who had been convicted of crimes during the past decade.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-53) The [First Amendment Coalition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Amendment_Coalition "First Amendment Coalition") stated about his position that it was "disheartening and ominous that the highest law enforcement officer in the state is threatening legal action over something the [First Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "First Amendment to the United States Constitution") makes clear can't give rise to criminal action".[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-54) One of the reporters stated that Becerra's legal threat was "just completely wrong in its interpretation of the law" and "had real implications for press freedom". The reporters ultimately published a number of articles about the records, and Becerra never prosecuted them.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-:1-55)

Becerra refused to offer independent investigation into the [killing of Sean Monterrosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killing_of_Sean_Monterrosa "Killing of Sean Monterrosa"), who had been shot in the back of the head by police. He later opposed a bill that would have required him to do so.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Intercept-56) Becerra said in a public statement that there were "significant" allegations of "destruction of evidence" in the case of Monterrosa's killing.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-57)

Two major state newspapers have criticized Becerra for, they stated, shielding law enforcement and lacking transparency. A number of news outlets stated that a significant part of his campaign support was provided by law enforcement unions.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Intercept-56) In a move that was criticized by his own party, Becerra refused to enforce a state law that required the government to release information about police officers accused of rape and physical abuse, ultimately resisting lawsuits for at least six years and despite having been ruled against by an appeals court.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-:1-55)

### Death penalty

During the [COVID-19 pandemic,](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic") Becerra acted to uphold a number of death penalty sentences.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Intercept-56) He stated in 2020 that he supported capital punishment with "serious reservations", while also stating that its applications were "deeply flawed" and that a number of "Americans have been wrongly sentenced to death in this country and later exonerated". He had earlier voted to repeal the death penalty in California in 2016. In 2017, he pursued the death penalty for a mass murderer. Becerra described Newsom’s 2019 decision to stop executions in the state as a "new direction in California's march toward perfecting our search for justice". The [Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times "Los Angeles Times") wrote in the same year that Becerra had "declined" to answer whether he supported capital punishment or not, stating only that the death penalty was part of the state law he had a duty to enforce. Two years later, his attorney general's office successfully argued to make it easier for juries to recommend death sentences, a position that Newsom argued against in court.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-:0-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-60)

An article by [Amherst College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amherst_College "Amherst College") professor [Austin Sarat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_Sarat "Austin Sarat") stated that Becerra had not, as attorney general, addressed the issues of "racial discrimination, the impact of geography, and the risk of false convictions" in California's death penalty cases.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-:0-59) Robert Lewis, a Black man with an IQ of 70, was sentenced to death in 1991, but was later ruled ineligible due to being intellectually disabled. In 2017, Becerra unsuccessfully sought to have a court artificially inflate Lewis' IQ score in order for him to be deemed eligible for the death penalty.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Intercept-56)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-:2-61)

While arguing in favor Lewis' death penalty eligibility in court, Becerra's office stated that his IQ score had been underestimated because Lewis' background was similar to that of "African American children [who] scored much more poorly on these tests than did the group against which the test was normed". Law professor [Lara Bazelon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lara_Bazelon "Lara Bazelon") described the argument as "alarming" and "race-based". The court ruled in favor of Lewis in a 7–0 decision.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-:2-61) Two years later, the state legislature banned the practice of adjusting IQ scoring based on race in death penalty cases.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Intercept-56)

### Lawsuits against Trump administration

#### Defense of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA)

In November 2019, Becerra led a coalition of 21 attorneys general to defend [DACA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DACA "DACA") against the Trump Administration's attempt to terminate it.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-62) The Court found that the administration's actions to end DACA were unlawful.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-63)

#### Defense of the Affordable Care Act (ACA)

Becerra led the multi-state lawsuit to preserve the ACA's protections for people with pre-existing conditions and Medicaid expansion. The Supreme Court upheld the law.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-65)

#### Additional federal litigation

In February 2019, Becerra, Governor Gavin Newsom, and 15 other states filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration over the president's [declaration of a national emergency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Emergency_Concerning_the_Southern_Border_of_the_United_States "National Emergency Concerning the Southern Border of the United States") to fund a wall at the southern U.S. border.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-66)

The Trump administration opened 1 million acres in California to [fracking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fracking "Fracking") and drilling in December 2019.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-67) Under this policy, the [Bureau of Land Management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bureau_of_Land_Management "Bureau of Land Management") proposed new lease sales for oil and gas extraction along "California's [Central Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Valley_(California) "Central Valley (California)") and [Central Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Coast_(California) "Central Coast (California)"), touching eight counties and including 400,000 acres of public land".[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Canon-68) California officials and agencies, including Becerra, filed a lawsuit against the Bureau of Land Management in January 2020.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-69)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Canon-68)

On December 9, 2020, Becerra's office joined 47 other states and the [Federal Trade Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Trade_Commission "Federal Trade Commission") in an antitrust lawsuit against [Facebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meta_Platforms "Meta Platforms").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-71)

### 2020 U.S. Senate speculation

In August 2020, California senator [Kamala Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris") was selected by presumptive Democratic presidential nominee [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") as his vice presidential running mate. After Biden ultimately won the [general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election "2020 United States presidential election"), Becerra was floated as a possible replacement for Harris' senate seat, along with others such as Representative [Karen Bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karen_Bass "Karen Bass"), Representative [Barbara Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Lee "Barbara Lee"), California Secretary of State [Alex Padilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Padilla "Alex Padilla") (who was eventually chosen), and former United States Secretary of Labor [Hilda Solis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilda_Solis "Hilda Solis").[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-72)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-74)

## U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services (2021–2025)

### Nomination and confirmation

*[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* reported in early December 2020 that Biden would nominate Becerra to be [secretary of health and human services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Secretary of Health and Human Services").[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-75) His nomination to lead the Health and Human Services Department drew criticism from pro-life and conservative leaders led by [Students for Life of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Students_for_Life_of_America "Students for Life of America"), citing his "absence of health care experience and his disregard for people of faith".[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-77) Becerra's nomination was deadlocked by the [Senate Finance Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Finance "United States Senate Committee on Finance") on March 10, 2021.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-78) One day later, on March 11, 2021, Becerra's nomination was discharged from the Finance Committee by the entire Senate, in a 51–48 vote.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-79) He was confirmed by the Senate in a 50–49 vote on March 18, 2021, with all but one Democrat present and one Republican, [Susan Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Collins "Susan Collins"), voting in favor.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-80)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-81) This was the narrowest vote for any of Biden's cabinet positions. On March 22, 2021, Becerra was sworn in to be the new secretary.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-82)

### Tenure

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/First_Lady_Jill_Biden_with_Secretary_Becerra_and_Secretary_McDonough.jpg/250px-First_Lady_Jill_Biden_with_Secretary_Becerra_and_Secretary_McDonough.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:First_Lady_Jill_Biden_with_Secretary_Becerra_and_Secretary_McDonough.jpg)Secretary Becerra with First Lady [Jill Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jill_Biden "Jill Biden") (center) and Secretary of Veterans Affairs [Denis McDonough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_McDonough "Denis McDonough") (left), June 4, 2021[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/V20220708CS-0462-Edit_%2852308683903%29.jpg/250px-V20220708CS-0462-Edit_%2852308683903%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:V20220708CS-0462-Edit_(52308683903).jpg)Becerra, Vice President [Kamala Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris"), and [Lisa Monaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisa_Monaco "Lisa Monaco") watch as President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") signs an executive order protecting access to reproductive healthcare service, July 8, 2022

Soon after officially becoming the secretary of health and human services, Becerra released a statement praising the [Affordable Care Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affordable_Care_Act "Affordable Care Act") and encouraging people to keep enrolling in its health care program.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-83)

After the Supreme Court's 2022 ruling in *[Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dobbs_v._Jackson_Women's_Health_Organization "Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization")*, Becerra directed HHS to expand access to abortion-related care where it could.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-84) Under his leadership the department also expanded [Medicaid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicaid "Medicaid") and [CHIP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children's_Health_Insurance_Program "Children's Health Insurance Program") postpartum coverage for more than half the states in the nation.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-85)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-86)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-87)

#### Medicare drug price negotiations

For Medicare beneficiaries, Becerra allowed direct price negotiations for high-cost medications under the [Inflation Reduction Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflation_Reduction_Act "Inflation Reduction Act"). In 2023, Becerra and HHS finalized negotiations for 10 high-cost drugs, including [Eliquis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliquis "Eliquis"), [Jardiance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jardiance "Jardiance"), and [Xarelto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xarelto "Xarelto"), achieving discounts of 38% to 79%. These lower prices, effective in 2026, would have saved Medicare $6 billion in 2023 alone.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-88) Later, Becerra announced 15 additional drugs for negotiation in 2025, with reduced prices set to take effect in 2027 for drugs that treat conditions such as cancer, diabetes, and asthma.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-89)

#### Unaccompanied migrant children

In his role, Becerra was responsible for the [Administration for Children and Families](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administration_for_Children_and_Families "Administration for Children and Families") and its [Office of Refugee Resettlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_Refugee_Resettlement "Office of Refugee Resettlement") (ORR) which is responsible for the care of unaccompanied minors after they cross the border. ORR typically places children in government shelters and screens adults who come forward to sponsor them,[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-90) a system which came under stress during Becerra's tenure due to an increase in border crossings. Employees told *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* that Becerra urged staff to move children through the processes faster and protections were loosened as a result.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-:3-91)

Over a two-year period, ORR could not reach about 85,000 children and reporting found that some of those children were working in jobs that are illegal for minors.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-:3-91) During a series of congressional oversight hearings, federal disclosures revealed that a safety hotline managed by the Office of Refugee Resettlement for unaccompanied migrant children had failed to respond to more than 65,000 calls and safety reports between August 2023 and January 2025.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-92) [Hannah Dreier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannah_Dreier "Hannah Dreier")'s series covering the events, titled "Alone and Exploited," won the 2024 [Pulitzer Prize for Investigative Reporting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize_for_Investigative_Reporting "Pulitzer Prize for Investigative Reporting").[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-93)

#### Additional matters

Becerra oversaw one of the biggest reform efforts of sub-agencies in HHS's history, including at the [Food and Drug Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_Drug_Administration "Food and Drug Administration")[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-94) and the [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control_and_Prevention "Centers for Disease Control and Prevention").[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-95)

Becerra was criticized as health and human services secretary for being absent in the public eye during the pandemic, for confusing messaging by federal public health authorities and for the subsequent loss of public trust, and for his collaborative management style while serving as secretary; his defenders said he was given an unclear role as secretary.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-96) Becerra was similarly criticized following his agency's response to the [2022 monkeypox outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_monkeypox_outbreak "2022 monkeypox outbreak") amid issues with health policy communication and what was widely considered a slow response; White House officials said that Becerra sought to [scapegoat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scapegoating "Scapegoating") the states rather than take responsibility for the subpar response.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-97)

In 2023, Becerra rejected cancer patients’ petition to use a law which allows HHS regulators to rescind exclusive patent protections for government-developed drugs making them more available to the generic market.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-98)

Becerra directed an overhaul of the national organ transplant system. In March 2023, the [Health Resources and Services Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_Resources_and_Services_Administration "Health Resources and Services Administration") announced a modernization initiative. The law ended the sole-source role that the [United Network for Organ Sharing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Network_for_Organ_Sharing "United Network for Organ Sharing") had held over the [Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organ_Procurement_and_Transplantation_Network "Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network") since 1986.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-99)

## 2026 California gubernatorial campaign

Main article: [2026 California gubernatorial election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_gubernatorial_election "2026 California gubernatorial election")

In the 2026 California gubernatorial election, [Gavin Newsom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavin_Newsom "Gavin Newsom") is ineligible to run for reelection as [governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_California "Governor of California") due to term limits. In February 2024, *[Politico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politico "Politico")* reported that Becerra was considering a run for governor, and that he or affiliated individuals had approached a political consulting firm to that effect.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Cadelago-100)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-101) On April 2, 2025, Becerra declared his candidacy for the election.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Cadelago-100)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-102) Three days after the primary election, on June 5, 2026, the [Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press") called Becerra as one of the top two candidates in the [primary election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_California#Procedure "Elections in California") that will advance to the general election in November.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-103) He will face Republican [Steve Hilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Hilton "Steve Hilton") in the general election.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-104)

In November 2025, *[Politico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politico "Politico")* reported on a scheme in which Becerra's closest aides, including his chief of staff of 20 years and Governor [Gavin Newsom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavin_Newsom "Gavin Newsom")'s former chief of staff, had siphoned money from his campaign accounts for years. The total amount was reported to be $225,000 over two years. Although Becerra was not accused of wrongdoing, *Politico* reported that he was facing scrutiny as to how he had not known about the situation until federal investigators approached him.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Politico-105) Becerra had previously faced criticism for suspected campaign finance violations; in 2024, it had been reported that he was paying $10,000 a month for campaign reporting from a dormant state account, an apparent [Hatch Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hatch_Act "Hatch Act") violation. Becerra stated that the expenditures were for account maintenance, which political experts stated to be "a very high cost to pay."[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-Politico-105)

## Personal life

Becerra is married to physician Carolina Reyes, and they have three daughters.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-106) He is a member of the [Inter-American Dialogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inter-American_Dialogue "Inter-American Dialogue") think tank, based in Washington, D.C.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-107) Becerra is Roman Catholic.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Becerra#cite_note-108)

**Dorothy Alanna Fink** is an American [endocrinologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endocrinology "Endocrinology") and government official who serves as the principal deputy [assistant secretary for health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assistant_Secretary_for_Health "Assistant Secretary for Health") since November 2025. She previously served as the acting [assistant secretary for health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assistant_Secretary_for_Health "Assistant Secretary for Health") from May 2025 to November 2025.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-1) She previously served as the acting [United States secretary of health and human services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Secretary of Health and Human Services") from January to February 2025. She is also the director of the [Office on Women's Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_on_Women's_Health "Office on Women's Health") in the [Department of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Department of Health and Human Services").

## Early life and education

Fink is the daughter of Robert and Karen Fink of [Johnstown, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnstown,_Pennsylvania "Johnstown, Pennsylvania"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-auto-2) where she graduated from [Westmont Hilltop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westmont_Hilltop_High_School "Westmont Hilltop High School") High School in 1999.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-3) She attended [Georgetown University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgetown_University "Georgetown University") where she focused on health studies.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-auto1-4) She received several awards as a student at Georgetown, including one for outstanding undergraduate research in chemistry, and she was also a *[USA Today](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USA_Today "USA Today")* Academic [All-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-American "All-American").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-auto-2)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-5) Fink once featured as a contestant on the Jan 17, 2007 episode of the long-running American television game show *[The Price Is Right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Price_Is_Right "The Price Is Right")*.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-6)

Fink received her medical degree from [Georgetown University School of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgetown_University_School_of_Medicine "Georgetown University School of Medicine"). She completed her combined internal medicine and pediatrics residency at the [University of Pittsburgh Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Pittsburgh_Medical_Center "University of Pittsburgh Medical Center"). She then completed a [National Institutes of Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institutes_of_Health "National Institutes of Health") post-doctoral fellowship in [endocrinology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endocrinology "Endocrinology") and metabolism at the [Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University_College_of_Physicians_and_Surgeons "Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons") in New York. During her fellowship, Fink was selected as a Women's Health Scholar and worked at the Center for Menopause, Hormonal Disorders and Women's Health. She has authored or co-authored 11 peer-reviewed articles on topics that include [thromboembolic disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thromboembolic_disease "Thromboembolic disease"), [diabetes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diabetes "Diabetes"), and [osteoporosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osteoporosis "Osteoporosis").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-auto1-4)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-7) Fink's [h-index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H-index "H-index"), a measure of her scholarly productivity and scientific impact, is reported to be 11.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-8)

Fink is board certified in endocrinology, [internal medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_medicine "Internal medicine"), and [pediatrics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pediatrics "Pediatrics"), and is recognized as a physician leader on topics such as diabetes, nutrition, and bone health. Previously, her clinical practice focused on women from adolescence through [menopause](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menopause "Menopause") and beyond. She is a nationally certified menopause practitioner and an expert on [estrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estrogen "Estrogen"). She has presented at several national meetings and has practiced at the [Hospital for Special Surgery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hospital_for_Special_Surgery "Hospital for Special Surgery") and the [NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NewYork-Presbyterian_Hospital "NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital"), [Cornell University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornell_University "Cornell University").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-auto1-4)

## Government official

### First Trump administration

In 2018, Fink was appointed by President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") as the deputy assistant secretary for women's health.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-9) In this role, Fink addressed the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") as part of the [UN Human Rights Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Human_Rights_Council "United Nations Human Rights Council") [Universal Periodic Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Periodic_Review "Universal Periodic Review"), a process that reviews the human rights records of member states, on the importance of reducing health disparities in minority populations.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-10) She also became the director of the [Office on Women's Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_on_Women's_Health "Office on Women's Health") in the [Department of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Department of Health and Human Services"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-auto1-4) lecturing on the importance of enhancing immunization culture, improving vaccine uptake, and combating vaccine misinformation.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-11)

### Second Trump administration

#### Acting Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services

On January 20, 2025, Fink was named by President Trump as the acting [United States Secretary of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Secretary of Health and Human Services"), as his nominee for the position, [Robert F. Kennedy Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_F._Kennedy_Jr. "Robert F. Kennedy Jr."), had not yet been approved by the [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-12) She immediately issued a January 21 memo titled "Immediate Pause on Issuing Documents and Publication Communications" [[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-14) forbidding U.S. health agency personnel from sending any document intended for publication to the Office of the *[Federal Register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Register "Federal Register")* until it has been reviewed and approved by a presidential appointee, publicly issuing any document or communication until it has been approved by a presidential appointee, and participating in public speaking engagements until the event and material have been reviewed and approved by a presidential appointee through February 1, 2025. The memo also required that health agency personnel coordinate with presidential appointees prior to issuing official correspondence to public officials, including that containing interpretations or statements of department regulations or policy. The effect of the action was to bring the work of HHS agencies (most importantly the [CDC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control_and_Prevention "Centers for Disease Control and Prevention"), [NIH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institutes_of_Health "National Institutes of Health"), and [FDA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_Drug_Administration "Food and Drug Administration")) to a virtual halt.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-15) Despite the February 1, 2025 expiration of the directives included in Fink's January 21 memo, the blocking of submissions to the *Federal Register* persists as of March 2, 2025, essentially halting all federal biomedical and public health research funding agencies, including the [National Institutes of Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institutes_of_Health "National Institutes of Health") (NIH).[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-:1-16)

On February 7, 2025, under the direction of Fink as acting HHS Secretary, the [National Institutes of Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institutes_of_Health "National Institutes of Health") issued new guidance on NIH grants[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-17) setting new, reduced, rates of support for the indirect costs of institutions performing NIH-sponsored research.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-18) Critics of the NIH policy shift included leading scientific and medical associations, with the sudden loss of funding described as "devastating", "apocalyptic", "disastrous" and "catastrophic".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-24) In response to the cuts, lawsuits were filed by attorneys general of twenty-two states, the [Association of American Medical Colleges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_American_Medical_Colleges "Association of American Medical Colleges"), the [Association of American Universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_American_Universities "Association of American Universities"), and other organizations representing leading biomedical research institutions, seeking an injunction to prevent the cuts from taking effect.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-25)

On February 10, 2025, U.S. District Judge Angel Kelley from the [District of Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_District_Court_for_the_District_of_Massachusetts "United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts") granted the plaintiff's motion for a temporary restraining order blocking Fink's policy from taking effect as planned.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-26) Fink, a named co-defendant in multiple lawsuits,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-33) filed a brief in opposition to the restraining order defending the drastic cuts in NIH funding.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-34) After a February 21 hearing, Judge Kelley extended the temporary restraining order pending a final ruling,[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-35) but major scientific research institutions have already begun to shutter laboratories, pause or rescind graduate student admissions,[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-37) and freeze hiring and spending in anticipation of what they view to be a potentially catastrophic policy taking effect, as well as other cuts in federal funding related to science and public health made by [Executive orders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_order "Executive order") issued by [President Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") or at the discretion of the [Department of Government Efficiency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Government_Efficiency "Department of Government Efficiency").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-41) On March 5, 2025, Judge Kelley ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, argued that NIH violated federal law and did not "contemplate the risk to human life as research and clinical trials are suspended in response" or "the life, careers, and advancement that will be lost as these budgets are indiscriminately slashed..."[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-42)

On February 18, 2025, it was reported that Fink and colleagues at HHS employed a new tactic to circumvent court orders enjoining the [Trump administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "Second presidency of Donald Trump")'s executive actions freezing Federal funding and cutting Congressionally allocated NIH-sponsored research. A leaked internal email sent to NIH personnel forbids NIH staff from submitting meeting notices to the *Federal Register*, the official journal of the United States Federal Government.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-43)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-:1-16) Meetings of study sections and advisory councils staffed by leading scientific expertise, which are responsible for reviewing NIH funding proposals and providing guidance to NIH on funding priorities, are required by law to post meeting plans in the *Federal Register* 15 days in advance of their scheduled date. Without being able to post meeting schedules in the *Federal Register*, new NIH grants cannot be reviewed or awarded.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-:1-16)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Fink#cite_note-44) As of March 5, 2025, no announcements of advisory council meetings have been posted, an action effectively halting the NIH grant award process.
